## {#four-problems data-menu-title="Four Problems"}

[Four things that went wrong]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
**No clear ownership**
Multiple people touched the same file — nobody claimed it

**Duplicate work**
Several PRs fixed the same problem — wasted effort

**Hard to track progress**
Who is working on what? Is that PR ready to merge?

**Confusing pull requests**
"Made some changes" — the reviewer has no idea what to look for
:::

---

## {#reframe data-menu-title="Reframe"}

[Git is not a save button]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Git is a **coordination system**.

| Git concept | What it really is |
|---|---|
| Commit | A record of a decision |
| Branch | A personal workspace with a purpose |
| Pull request | A conversation about whether a change belongs |
| Issue | A defined unit of work with an owner |
| Project board | A shared view of the project's state |
:::

---

## {#five-people data-menu-title="Five People"}

[The five-people problem]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Imagine five people editing the same document at once:

**Who owns what?**
If everyone can edit everything, nobody is responsible for anything.

**What if two people change the same sentence?**
Both versions exist — who decides which is right?

**How do you know what changed?**
Without a record, you cannot trace a decision back to its source.
:::

::: {.body-text}
GitHub solves all three — but only if you use it with intention.
:::

---

## {#branches-intro data-menu-title="Branches Intro"}

[Main branch = the official version]{.slide-title}

::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="55%"}
![](../../images/github_collaboration/allison-horst-jenny-bryan-quote.png){width=100%}
::::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.body-text}
**`main`** is the published version — clean, reviewed, trusted.

You do not edit `main` directly.

**Branches** are personal workspaces.
Create one when you start a task.
Work there safely.
Nothing touches `main` until it has been reviewed.
:::
::::

:::

---

## {#branch-workflow data-menu-title="Branch Workflow"}

[The five-step branch workflow]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
1. **Create a branch**
2. **Make your changes**
3. **Open a pull request**
4. **Review**
5. **Merge**

Everything we add today is in service of making
these five steps *intentional* rather than chaotic.
:::

---

## {#what-is-pr data-menu-title="What Is a PR"}

[What a pull request actually is]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
You are **not** saying:

> *"I changed the file."*

You are **asking**:

> *"Here is my version — should we accept it?"*
:::

::: {.body-text}
A pull request is a proposal. It invites review, discussion,
and a deliberate decision about whether the change belongs.

**The commit is the work. The pull request is the conversation about the work.**
:::

---

## {#pr-writing data-menu-title="Writing a PR"}

[Writing and reviewing pull requests]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
**If you are writing a PR:**

Make the case for your change.
What did you do? Why? What should the reviewer look for?

**If you are reviewing a PR:**

Actually engage with the change.
Does it do what it claims? Is there a better approach?
Are there side effects?

"Looks good" is not a review.
:::

---

[In the chat]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
**In your own words:**

What is the difference between a commit and a pull request?

One sentence.
:::

## {#issues-intro data-menu-title="Issues Intro"}

[Issues: defining the work]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
An **issue** is a defined unit of work.

- Has a title, a description, and an assignee
- One issue = one task
- Specific, bounded, completable

**The rule: no work without an issue.**

Before you touch a file, there is an issue that describes what
you are doing and why — and it is assigned to you.

This solves the ownership problem.
:::

---

## {#issue-examples data-menu-title="Issue Examples"}

[What makes a good issue?]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
❌ Too vague

> "Improve the analysis"

✅ Specific and completable

> "Add axis labels to the species richness plot"

> "Fix the broken file path in the data loading script"

> "Add a methods section to the draft report"
:::

---

## {#project-board data-menu-title="Project Board"}

[Project board: seeing the whole picture]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Four columns track every piece of work:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **To Do** | Available — not yet claimed |
| **In Progress** | Claimed — someone is working on it |
| **In Review** | PR is open — waiting for review |
| **Done** | Merged — issue closed |
:::

::: {.body-text}
At any moment, anyone can see the full state of the project
without asking anyone.
:::

---

## {#full-workflow data-menu-title="Full Workflow"}

[The structured workflow — ten steps]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
1. Go to Issues → choose one → assign yourself
2. Move to **In Progress** on the board
3. Create a branch: `issue-#-short-description`
4. Make your change — one task only
5. Commit with a clear message
6. Push and open a PR — write `Closes #[issue number]`
7. Move to **In Review** on the board
8. Partner reviews PR — leaves at least 2 specific comments
9. Revise if needed → merge
10. Move issue to **Done**
:::

---

## {#closes-syntax data-menu-title="Closes Syntax"}

[What does `Closes #3` do?]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
In the chat: **take a guess**.
:::

. . .

::: {.body-text}
When the PR merges, GitHub **automatically closes issue #3**.

It also links the PR to the issue in the UI — you can
click from one to the other.

This is the automation payoff for using issues and PRs together.
:::

---

## {#branch-naming data-menu-title="Branch Naming"}

[Branch naming is communication]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Name your branch: `issue-#-short-description`

Examples:

- `issue-3-fix-readme`
- `issue-7-add-axis-labels`
- `issue-12-fix-data-path`

The issue number in the branch name tells anyone on the
team exactly what the branch is for — without asking.

Compare to: `my-edits`, `updates`, `patch-1`
:::

---

## {#workflow-rules data-menu-title="Workflow Rules"}

[The rules]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
**No work without an issue**
Claim it before you start.

**No direct edits to `main`**
Always work on a branch.

**One issue per branch**
If you notice another problem, open a new issue.

**Every PR must be reviewed before merging**
"Looks good" is not a review.
:::

## {#workflow-summary data-menu-title="Workflow Summary"}

[The structured workflow — summary]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
```
Issue → Assign → In Progress
    ↓
Branch (issue-#-name)
    ↓
Edit → Commit → Push
    ↓
Pull Request (Closes #X) → In Review
    ↓
Review → Revise → Merge
    ↓
Done
```
:::

---

## {#key-takeaways-wed data-menu-title="Key Takeaways Wednesday"}

[Three things to remember]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
**1.** Git is a coordination system, not a save button.
Every branch, commit, PR, and issue is a communication tool.

**2.** Structure prevents chaos.
Monday felt messy because there was no structure —
not because the tools are hard.

**3.** Pull requests are conversations.
Write them so the reviewer knows what to look for.
Review them so the author knows what you actually looked at.
:::
